mark 1 · 15% less time 275°F / 135°C Gas mark 1 · 10% less time What recipes use 160°C 160°C (320°F, gas mark 3) is the low, gentle heat for anything that must set slowly without browning: baked custards, cheesecakes, meringues, terrines, and slow-roasted tomatoes. It is also the temperature for reheating delicate leftovers in the oven. A general recipe converts to 145°C in a basket air fryer. The cut is smaller than at higher temperatures because these foods need the heat to reach the centre gently. The failure mode at 160°C: unset centre, browned top At this temperature the risk is not burning — it is that the moving air browns the top before the centre sets. A cheesecake or custard will crack and dome while the middle is still liquid. Use a water bath if the recipe calls for one, tent loosely with foil, and test the centre at the check time with a skewer or thermometer. In a basket air fryer the fan is closer to the food, so the tent is essential. Worked example (conventional) A cheesecake recipe says 160°C for 30 minutes. Baked custards take a small cut, so a basket air fryer runs it at 150°C (300°F) for 26 minutes; test the centre at 18 minutes. An oven-style unit blows less directly onto the top, so it takes 150°C (305°F) for 27 minutes. Bake in a springform pan set on the crisper plate, tented with foil. Worked example (fan) If the recipe gives a fan temperature of 140°C, the same cheesecake converts to 130°C (270°F) in a basket air fryer for 29 minutes, checked at 20 minutes. An oven-style unit runs 135°C (275°F) for 30 minutes. The fan input goes through the convection engine, which takes a gentler cut because the recipe is already fan-adjusted. Why the recipe prints three temperatures UK and EU recipes often write "160°C / 140°C fan / gas mark 3". The conventional figure is for a non-fan oven; the fan figure is roughly 20°C lower because the fan moves heat faster. gas mark 3 is the UK dial setting (~160°C). Pick the one your recipe uses: conventional goes through the flagship engine, fan goes through the convection engine, gas mark maps to the conventional °C. The converter widget on this page lets you switch between them. For frozen food packs (which print one time for both conventional and fan), use the frozen mode instead — it keeps the temperature and cuts the time by 30%. For a general recipe, 145°C (295°F) in a basket air fryer with about 20% less time, or 150°C in an oven-style unit. Custards and slow bakes take a smaller cut; see the table. My recipe says 140°C fan — is that the same as 160°C conventional? Yes, that is the UK convention: fan = conventional − 20°C. Use the fan input on this page (or the convection converter) for a fan-oven recipe; it takes a gentler cut because the recipe is already adjusted for the fan. What gas mark is 160°C? gas mark 3. The UK dial marks 160°C as gas mark 3. Can I use this for a frozen food pack that says 160°C? No — frozen packs follow different rules (keep the temperature, cut 30% time). Use the frozen mode on this site instead; it handles conventional and fan pack temperatures correctly. Why does the fan column give a different answer from the conventional column? A fan-oven recipe is already 20°C lower than its conventional equivalent. The convection engine applies a smaller cut (0–15°F, 5–10% time) because the fan has already done part of the work. The conventional engine applies the full cut (20–25°F, 20–30% time).
